```{r}
#| label: setup
library(here)
library(readr)
library(knitr)
here::i_am("checkpoint1.qmd")
data_dir <- here::here("data")
out_dir <- here::here("output")
dir.create(out_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
stopifnot(length(list.files(file.path(data_dir, "set-a"), pattern = "[.]txt$")) == 4000)
```

```{r}
#| label: load-analysis
status <- system2("python", "scripts/run_analysis.py")
stopifnot(status == 0)
```

## Cohort and outcome summary

The source contains one ICU admission per record file. The analysis preserves the source `-1` code in the raw-value column and treats it as missing for summaries. Table 1 summarizes admissions, not repeated measurements.

```{r}
#| label: table1
table1 <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "table1.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(table1, caption = "Table 1. Set-a cohort characteristics")
```

```{r}
#| label: outcomes
outcomes <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "outcome_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
death <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "death_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(outcomes, caption = "Outcome summary: continuous outcomes")
knitr::kable(death, caption = "Outcome summary: in-hospital death")
```

## Long and wide tables

The long table retains original time, numeric hours after admission, parameter, raw value, and analysis value. The wide table has one row per admission and count, first, last, minimum, maximum, and mean summaries for dynamic variables over 0–48 hours. Missing values are not replaced by zero.

```{r}
#| label: table-checks
long <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "set-a_long.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
wide <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "set-a_wide.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
data.frame(metric = c("long rows", "unique admissions", "variables", "time minimum", "time maximum", "wide rows"), value = c(nrow(long), dplyr::n_distinct(long$RecordID), dplyr::n_distinct(long$Parameter), min(long$time_hours), max(long$time_hours), nrow(wide))) |> knitr::kable(caption = "Derived-table checks")
quality <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "data_quality_summary.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(quality, caption = "Data-quality checks")
```

## Missingness maps

In an event-style long table, no row for a variable and interval represents no observed measurement. The six-hour map displays temporal measurement presence. The wide-table map displays missingness after admission-level aggregation.

```{r}
#| label: missingness
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
knitr::include_graphics(c(file.path(out_dir, "figures", "long_missingness_map.png"), file.path(out_dir, "figures", "variable_time_measurement_rate.png"), file.path(out_dir, "figures", "wide_missingness_map.png")))
informative <- readr::read_csv(file.path(out_dir, "missingness_by_outcome.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(head(informative[order(-informative$never_measured_n), ], 20), caption = "Death rate by whether a variable was ever measured")
```

## Modeling objective and AI-use statement

The eventual mortality model will be assessed using the smaller of sensitivity and positive predictive value, `min(TP/(TP+FN), TP/(TP+FP))`, so poor performance on either missed deaths or false positive alerts is penalized. The Hosmer–Lemeshow statistic will assess calibration by comparing observed and expected deaths across risk groups. No model is fitted in this checkpoint.

GPT/Codex assisted with project setup, interpretation of submission requirements, code drafting, debugging, and explanations of Python, Git, pixi, missingness, and clinical variables. I reviewed the generated code, checked source paths and formats, and used assertions plus reproducible outputs to inspect results. AI can accelerate iteration but may introduce incorrect assumptions or silent transformations, so the final document and generated tables must be reviewed against the source data.
